newsitem.title: ROMANIA: THEATRE GROUPS EAGER TO REVIVE YIDDISH LANGUAGE.
newsitem.headline: THEATRE GROUPS EAGER TO REVIVE YIDDISH LANGUAGE.

text.p: The Yiddish language has been doomed by history and demography, but groups from throughout Europe and Israel have a mission to revive and develop it.

Actors at the Festival of Jewish Theatres converged on Bucharest for the second year with the single-minded aim of defending the language of European Jewry, rooted in the Middle Ages but pushed into the background in the modern state of Israel in favour of Hebrew.
Bucharest's polished Jewish State Theatre played host to groups from Ukraine, France and Israel.
Many of the actors have no Jewish background but learn enough to play their parts -- often coached by one of the troupe's few native speakers.
"I've been Jewish for about four years now," joked Iulia Gavril, a regular performer at the Bucharest theatre.
"I came to this theatre because the working atmosphere was so good. No sniping, no bad feeling."
Constantin Dinulescu, a distinguished Romanian actor, learned from scratch his role as an elderly rabbi in "Uriel Acosta", a 19th century tragedy about a Jew who refuses to recant.
"People keep complimenting me on my Yiddish," he said. "I grew up in Iasi (northeastern Romania) where there was a large Jewish community. I suppose some of the language rubbed off."
Scholars agree Yiddish is fighting a losing battle.
"I don't realistically think Yiddish will ever be a widely spoken language again," Chava Turmiansky, head of the Yiddish department at Jerusalem's Hebrew University, said by telephone.
"You can do a lot to preserve and cherish it and maybe one day we may see a revival. But this isn't happening now. Linguistic assimilation has been going on for some time."

Turmiansky said it was impossible to determine how many people speak Yiddish, which sounds something like German peppered with phrases reflecting local language and custom wherever Jews happened to live.
"It's unclear. Statistics are compounded by the fact that many Jews spoke two and three other languages," he said.
"You can't even say that the six million Jews in the Holocaust were Yiddish speakers. No Yiddish was spoken in Hungary or Germany for instance."
Yiddish was abandoned in Israel because of its association with ghettos and because Sephardic Jews from the Middle East and Africa did not speak it.
Its regular use there is confined generally to tightly-knit Orthodox communities who reject Hebrew as a secular tongue.
Yiddish-speakers can be found throughout Europe, North America and Argentina, but are becoming fewer and older.
Newspapers close for lack of leadership. The world's last daily Unzer Wort ceased publication in Paris this year and two papers in Israel appear only twice a week.
The Bucharest festival exposed a raw debate on the strategy of reviving the language -- performing traditional Jewish works or attracting new audiences with a more modern approach.
Tel Aviv's "Yiddish Spiel" group performed traditional songs guaranteed to make any Jewish mother weep.
Its directors call for maintaining the "roots" of Yiddish song and literature and offered help to others struggling against long cultural and often financial odds.
The Romanians, Ukrainians and French disagreed and called for change.
"We can't behave as though we were living in a museum like in the past," Harry Eliad, Bucharest theatre director, told a discussion group. "We have to get people to learn Yiddish through new means."
Georgy Melsky's young, and penniless, Mazltov troupe from Kiev consists mainly of inexperienced but hard-working actors in their twenties fresh out of university.
"It's not easy performing in a Yiddish-language theatre in Ukraine but we try hard," said Kiril Bin after a performance of a modern medley of songs and verse called "I am a Jew".
"Some of us are Jewish but most aren't. We don't even have a theatre and there certainly aren't any government grants. But trying to preserve this language is a noble cause."
Melsky has more mundane concerns. He had to rely on donations to bring his troupe to Bucharest.
"My government gives me plenty of awards but no place to perform," he said. "I would normally come with far more actors, but we just didn't have the money. Can't you see we need help?"
Performers in France have things easier, but not much.

"Sure it's hard to be a Yiddish-language actor in France. There's simply no one to perform with," said Rafael Goldwasser, an Argentine-born Jew who works in Strasbourg and put on a one-man show at the festival.

"So I do bilingual performances and of course perform in other theatres too. But it's like a spark. If you blow on it the fire won't go out. Certain small details remain deep in my subconscious and that's what I draw on for my performances."
